caption:
Jack Dorsey's Block unveiled Dessa, a voice AI trained only on recordings of people talking, with no text at all.
It listens and speaks at the same time, so it can interrupt, laugh and react mid-sentence.
Block says it runs on a MacBook Pro, but for now only a few safety researchers get access.

Would you be able to tell you were talking to an AI?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Notebookcheck
threads_text: Jack Dorsey's Block built a voice AI that never saw a single written word. It learned only from recordings of people talking, and Block says it runs on a MacBook. Amazing tech, or a gift to phone scammers?

paragraphs.text: Block, the payments company led by Jack Dorsey that runs Square and Cash App, unveiled a voice model called Dessa on October 23, 2026. According to Block, the model was trained from scratch using only recordings of human conversation, without any written text and without starting from a pretrained language model.

Dessa is described as a full duplex speech to speech system. It takes in audio and produces audio directly instead of converting speech to text first, and it can listen and talk at the same time. That lets it interrupt, acknowledge what a speaker is saying and react before the other person finishes, as people do on a phone call.

Block says Dessa learned language from hundreds of times fewer words than conventional text based language models need. The company has not published the comparison behind that claim, and Kingy AI noted that no protocol for it was given.

The company presented the idea through a comparison with infants, who learn to speak before they can read. Crypto Briefing reported that Block framed the project as a test of whether a model can pick up language the same way. The Dessa team also said that current AI systems are largely unable to register the emotion in human voices, and named that gap as a reason for the work.

According to Block, the model was trained on a single NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 system, a rack scale machine that NVIDIA specifies with 72 Blackwell GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs. Block also says Dessa runs locally on a MacBook Pro with Apple's M4 Max chip or better, with inference faster than real time and no cloud servers required. None of these hardware claims has been independently verified.

Block posted recorded conversations on its website and said they capture live interactions in which no one steered the model, with subtitles added afterward. In the clips, Dessa laughs mid sentence, speaks louder when asked, helps a speaker who is struggling to recall a movie title and holds a conversation with OpenAI's GPT-Live-1 voice model.

Some recordings also show limits. Reports noted moments where the model misidentified a speaker, took over a speaker's turn or changed topics unexpectedly. Because Block selected the clips itself, outlets including Notebookcheck cautioned that they should be treated as first party material.

Dessa was built by a small research lab inside Block led by Ragavan Thurairatnam that reports directly to Dorsey. Reports said the lab was founded by former members of Dessa, a deep learning startup based in Toronto.

The model is a research preview, not a product. Block is offering early access to a small group of AI safety researchers, and others can join a waitlist. The company has not disclosed the parameter count, model weights, benchmark results, pricing or a public release date.

Reaction online mixed admiration for how natural the voice sounds with concern about misuse. NewsCord, which compared coverage from ten outlets, reported that some commentators warned a convincing human sounding voice could make phone scams harder to spot.

Most voice assistants are built on top of text models, so they inherit the turn taking rhythm of a chatbot: wait, transcribe, answer. A model trained only on audio could, in principle, pick up timing, tone and hesitation that text never records. The claims about efficiency and laptop performance are what make Dessa notable, and they are also the claims that outside researchers have not yet been able to test.
The next signal is whether Block publishes weights, a paper or benchmark results, which would let independent researchers check its claims about training without text and running on a laptop.
